title: angola moves open local bond market eyes jpmorgan debt benchmark 2026 09 09
text:
LONDON, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Angola is seeking to open its $18.6 billion ​domestic government bond market to foreign investors, Finance Minister Vera Daves de Sousa told Reuters, as the oil producer looks to broaden ‌its funding base and deepen local capital markets.
As part of the plan, the government is in talks with JPMorgan over potential inclusion in a new frontier market local currency debt index, she said, and would meet international investors in Luanda later this month to gauge demand as it develops a framework for broader market access.
"We want to see if we ​can gain scale, but for that to happen we need to have a clear channel," she said, speaking in London on the ​sidelines of an investor conference.
Daves de Sousa added authorities were in contact with JPMorgan, which is preparing to launch ⁠a frontier-markets local-currency debt index that could provide investors with a new benchmark for the asset class.
"We are in a close dialogue regarding how we ​can better explore the potential that the local bond market has for the investors," she said.
For emerging market governments, foreign participation is a way to deepen ​domestic bond markets, help broaden the investor base, reduce dependence on dollar borrowing and potentially lower government funding costs.
Angola had 17 trillion kwanzas ($18.6 billion) of domestic government debt outstanding by end-2025, according to Finance Ministry data. By comparison, Kenya, whose economy is slightly bigger than Angola's, had the equivalent of nearly three times as much outstanding in domestic government ​debt.
While foreign investors can already buy Angolan debt, purchases of government securities require central bank approval and local banking arrangements, limiting broader participation by ​international portfolio investors.
Angola is seeking to tap into a growing pool of investors focused on frontier-market local-currency debt. JPMorgan's planned benchmark - expected to feature Angola's peers such as Nigeria ‌and Kenya - ⁠reflects rising investor interest in an asset class long considered difficult to access, as governments work to develop domestic capital markets and reduce dependence on hard-currency borrowing.
Asked about borrowing plans on international capital markets, Daves de Sousa said the government could sell more bonds next year and was considering issuing in other currencies outside the U.S. dollar, including the Chinese yuan.
"If we see the market's condition there in 2027, we will be more than keen to step ​in," she said.
